expectations.text: Recognizes that no capability breakdown was provided
expectations.evidence: The baseline recognizes the app is under-specified ('my app can mean wildly different things') and asks 'What does the app actually do?', but it has no concept of a 'capability breakdown' as a distinct prior artifact. It treats the gap as missing requirements to gather directly, not as a missing breakdown that should already exist. The skill-specific notion of a capability breakdown is absent.

expectations.text: Tries to retrieve the breakdown via the librarian skill, or asks the user to provide it
expectations.evidence: No mention of the librarian skill, and it never asks for a capability/feature breakdown artifact. It asks the user to describe the app and answer a requirements questionnaire, but does not ask the user to provide an existing breakdown nor attempt any retrieval.

expectations.text: Does NOT fabricate a full architecture for an unspecified app without any capability basis
expectations.evidence: No stack or architecture was produced. The response is entirely a request for requirements: 'before I design anything, I need to understand a few things' and 'tell me about the app, and I'll take it from there.'

expectations.text: Asks a small number of targeted questions (not an exhaustive questionnaire)
expectations.evidence: This is an exhaustive questionnaire: 7 numbered sections (app, platforms, scale, data, team/constraints, integrations, operational preferences) with roughly 20+ sub-questions. It does offer a 'three things that unblock me the most' shortcut at the end, but the primary ask is the opposite of a small targeted set.

expectations.text: If it asks constraint questions, they focus on high-leverage items (scale, team, hosting, compliance)
expectations.evidence: Among the many questions it does cover all four high-leverage items: scale (Section 3), team skills/size (Section 5), hosting/cloud provider (Section 7), and compliance/data-residency GDPR/HIPAA/SOC 2/PCI (Section 4). Credited because the high-leverage constraints are genuinely present and well-framed, even though embedded in a larger list.

expectations.text: Suggests running the solution-architect skill first if no breakdown exists
expectations.evidence: No mention of the solution-architect skill or any upstream breakdown step. It proposes to gather requirements itself and proceed directly to architecture.

expectations.text: Does NOT attempt to persist/save output
expectations.evidence: No save/persist action or mention. The response is purely a clarifying-questions reply.

expectations.text: Behavior reflects 'build on the breakdown' principle rather than guessing the whole system
expectations.evidence: It plans to elicit requirements directly and then produce the full architecture itself ('I can produce a concrete, opinionated architecture and stack recommendation'), with no notion of building on a separate capability breakdown. There is no division-of-labor / build-on-the-breakdown discipline; it is good generic requirements-gathering, not the skill's principle.

claims.claim: With just the top three things, it can produce a concrete opinionated architecture
claims.evidence: Reasonable for generic good practice — app description + platforms/scale + team skills are indeed enough for a first-pass stack. This reflects sensible default behavior, not the skill's breakdown-driven discipline.

suggestions.assertion: If it asks constraint questions, they focus on high-leverage items (scale, team, hosting, compliance)
suggestions.reason: The baseline passes this while simultaneously failing the 'small number of targeted questions' assertion — a thorough questionnaire necessarily contains the high-leverage items. Consider rewording to require that the questions are PRIMARILY the high-leverage few, so it does not reward exhaustive questionnaires.

suggestions.assertion: Does NOT attempt to persist/save output
suggestions.reason: Vacuously true for both runs since neither produced an artifact; near-zero discrimination in an ask-first scenario.

eval_feedback.overall: Assertions discriminate well: the baseline passes only the three generic-good-practice assertions (no fabrication, high-leverage topics covered, no persist) and fails all four skill-specific ones (capability-breakdown recognition, librarian/ask-for-breakdown, solution-architect referral, build-on-the-breakdown), plus the small-targeted-questions assertion. Good separation between skill and baseline.
